Yes power is the bottleneck but even for power generating (including mining sites targeting conversion efforts)

There are several important considerations that determine the quality of the HPC energy pipeline.

———

1. Cooling issue: liquid cooling 
Bitcoin miners are mostly air-cooled. AI GPUs (H100-class and especially newer rack-scale systems) generate far higher heat and rack densities that air cooling cannot support.

•Mining racks commonly run ~5–15 kW on air.
•AI racks reach ~40 kW (H100) and 120–140+ kW (GB200 NVL72 and similar), with liquid cooling becoming required above roughly 30–40 kW.
•Direct-to-chip liquid cooling (or immersion) is needed. So, water loops, CDUs, heat exchangers, and cooling towers

Effective rebuild of the mechanical plant of the facility.

AI’s seem to agree that Air-cooled mining sheds do not retrofit cleanly; the cooling system is usually replaced rather than adapted.

2. Structural issue: Weight GPU racks with liquid cooling systems are significantly heavier than air-cooled mining rigs.

•Fully loaded liquid-cooled AI racks commonly weigh 3k-8k+ lbs.
•means reinforcement of floors, foundations, or supports is often necessary.

3. Power issue: Topology and Redundancy 
Mining sites are built for maximum continuous draw and tolerate power dips or interruptions. AI tenants require high-availability power.

•Mining facilities typically have minimal or no redundancy (N), no UPS, and little or no backup generation.
•Hyperscalers / AI tenants generally require Tier II or Tier III equivalence (N+1 or dual-path / approaching 2N), with UPS systems and backup generators sized to 1.2–2× critical IT load so servers never go down.
•This usually means replacing or adding expensive electrical switchgear, generators, UPS, and dual feeds.
•Existing interconnection and substation capacity can be reused; the internal power topology and redundancy layer almost always needs redesign.

4. Real estate issue: Fiber and Latency Mining can operate in remote locations with minimal connectivity. AI inference and training require high-bandwidth, low-latency fiber.

•Mining needs only low bandwidth (sometimes just cellular).
•AI requires dark fiber laterals plus high-speed internal fabrics (e.g., InfiniBand); rural sites chosen purely for cheap power usually disqualified outright or face major fiber build costs and timelines.
•Training is somewhat more latency-tolerant than inference, but both still need substantial connectivity.

Honorable mentions
•Grid-level interconnection and power-purchase agreements (existing firm power and interconnection position are usually the most valuable assets).
•High-voltage transmission access and substation capacity.
•Jurisdiction incentives that support conversion or new build-out.
•Water availability and permitting for cooling systems.

Five Surprising Truths About the $4 Trillion AI Wipeout, the Midterm Sweep, and the Fight for Compute

Watch a $4 trillion tech sell-off collide with a historic midterm blowout, and the obvious headline writes itself. Voters punished the party in power over the war in Iran and 3.7% inflation, while Wall Street panicked over incoming governors freezing data center permits. Yet beneath those surface explanations, the hosts of the All-In Podcast uncovered a far more surprising set of economic and technological shifts that explain where power and money are actually moving next.

1. Political Ideology Lost to the K-Shaped Economy

For decades, party strategists trusted two tools to win elections: massive campaign war chests and aggressive gerrymandering. In the 2026 midterms, both failed completely. In races across Texas and Ohio, millions of dollars in campaign spending went to waste, to the point where betting on the candidate with no money was the smarter play. Even more striking, out of 15 congressional districts specifically redrawn by Republicans to guarantee GOP victories, Democrats captured 11 seats while Republicans won just one.

Chamath Palihapitiya argues this happened because voters have moved past party loyalty altogether. Since the pandemic doubled federal spending and inflated asset prices, the country has split into a small group of asset owners who profit in every market condition and a much larger group of wage earners losing purchasing power.

   "There is a small percentage of people, the four of us on this pod and all of our friends, who are the asset owners of America, and we have benefited in every weather condition."

Voters delivered massive mandates to Biden, then to Trump, and now to congressional Democrats. Rather than endorsing left-wing or right-wing ideology, a central bloc of Americans is swinging back and forth against the status quo, firing whichever party fails to fix the daily cost of living.

2. Americans Dislike AI More Than Almost Any Country on Earth

The United States builds the world's leading artificial intelligence, yet Americans are deeply pessimistic about what the technology means for their future. According to a global Gallup study highlighted by David Friedberg, 93% of citizens in China believe AI will mostly help people and improve their daily lives. In the United States, that number sits at just 36%, placing Americans fourth from last in the world, trailing Afghanistan and sitting just ahead of Malawi and Bangladesh.

That resentment has turned physical data centers into a populist target, regardless of the actual local math. When two SpaceX employees recently presented plans for a 6-gigawatt data center in Cochise County, Arizona, they explained that the project would use zero water, cut local electricity costs by 40%, lower property taxes by 20%, and pay off a county bond. Local residents screamed over the presenters anyway.

When wage earners hear that GDP and the stock market are hitting record highs while their own grocery and utility bills climb, they assume tech billionaires are hoarding all the economic growth. Watching trillion-dollar companies demand local tax breaks to build $50 billion facilities only pours fuel on that anger.

3. Freezing Data Centers Actually Helps Big Tech Monopolies

Incoming leaders like Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa have vowed to pause new data center permits to rein in tech oligarchs, and David Sacks warns that a literal permit freeze could even strand half-built facilities waiting on final air pollution approvals. The counter-intuitive reality is that a construction slowdown hurts AI startups while making the biggest tech giants much stronger.

Foundational model builders like OpenAI and Anthropic, along with neocloud providers, belong to a vulnerable renter class. They lack fortress balance sheets and must rent compute capacity to keep their 60-to-90-day model improvement loops running. Meanwhile, hyperscalers like Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and SpaceX already control the existing power and infrastructure. Google recently took over a Crusoe data center simply because Google controlled the underlying power.

If new permits dry up, hyperscalers can hoard incremental compute for their own models or hike prices across the board. Chamath points out that SpaceX holds a mutual 90-day termination clause in its compute contract with Anthropic. If compute scarcity pushes spot prices up two or three times higher, spreadsheet logic will force SpaceX to terminate the old agreement and reprice that capacity, triggering a desperate buying panic among neoclouds trying to avoid bankruptcy.

4. Permitting Delays Will Push AI Offshore and Onto Your Desktop

State governors who treat data centers like captive local factories are about to learn a painful lesson about modern internet infrastructure. Because global fiber cables, content delivery networks, and Starlink move data around the world effortlessly, AI training does not need to happen on American soil.

Jason Calacanis warns that domestic permitting freezes will push $50 billion data centers to Canada, Mexico, Singapore, Malaysia, and the Middle East, or even into orbit with SpaceX. Instead of collecting local tax revenue and keeping $300,000-to-$400,000 construction jobs at home, the United States risks becoming a net importer of digital tokens.

At the same time, businesses are preparing to bypass cloud bottlenecks on their own. At his 20-person venture firm, LAUNCH, spending $40,000 to $50,000 a year on subscriptions like Claude and Grok already generates $1 million in incremental revenue and $2 million in value. Because everyday business workflows only require 70% to 80% of a frontier model's capabilities, Calacanis plans to spend $400,000 to buy every employee a $20,000 Mac Studio. Running open-source models locally on desktop hardware guarantees unmetered intelligence without waiting on a politician to approve a power plant.

5. A 27-Year-Old Computer Science Barrier Just Fell in a Few Hours

While Washington debates whether to create a federal Department of AI to police frontier models, the technology itself is quietly solving problems that stumped human mathematicians for a generation. Since 1999, computer scientists have relied on the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which stated that a core category of logic problems known as 3-SAT scales exponentially in difficulty and can never be solved quickly by a computer.

OpenAI just disproved that 27-year-old hypothesis in a 175-page paper. Even more remarkable than the proof itself is the speed of the discovery: OpenAI generated the breakthrough end-to-end in less than 10 days, with some reports indicating the work took just a few hours.

By demonstrating that 3-SAT problems can be solved in subexponential time, OpenAI kept alive the famous $P = NP$ question, which asks whether every problem whose answer can be quickly checked can also be quickly solved. If that holds true, almost every complex problem in the universe is theoretically computable.

The collision between populist politics and advancing technology has created a strange paradox for the next two years. Voters are demanding immediate relief on gas, groceries, housing, and utility bills, while the machines inside those controversial data centers are beginning to crack foundational mysteries of science. 

If American leaders freeze the physical infrastructure of intelligence to win a short-term fight over local tax breaks, what happens when the rest of the world builds the future without us?

Key Takeaways

   - Economics Over Ideology: Voters bypassed party loyalty, campaign spending, and gerrymandering in the midterms to punish the party in power over a K-shaped economy that favors asset owners over wage earners.

   - The Data Center Paradox: Although only 36% of Americans view AI positively, state-level permitting freezes will actually consolidate power among giant hyperscalers, push data center construction overseas, and accelerate local desktop AI adoption.

   - Accelerating Scientific Value: Despite public skepticism and regulatory threats, OpenAI's rapid 175-page disproof of the 27-year-old Exponential Time Hypothesis demonstrates that AI is already solving generational problems in computer science.

Someone is building a free, open-source alternative to professional 3D texture-painting software. And the entire application is written in Rust. 🎨

Meet TextureCraft, a new 3D painting application from the ArtCraft team.

Instead of painting textures in Photoshop and constantly checking how they look on a 3D model, TextureCraft allows artists to work directly on the object's surface.

It combines familiar texture-painting workflows with modern GPU acceleration and an unusually broad collection of file formats.

🎮 What can it do?

▪️ Direct 3D painting: Paint materials on a mesh while viewing the actual surface.

▪️ Layer-based workflow: Work with texture sets, layer stacks, masks, and per-channel blending.

▪️ Smart materials: Generate realistic wear, dirt, curvature effects, and other details using procedural masks.

▪️ Mesh baking: Generate ambient occlusion, curvature, thickness, and other mesh maps.

▪️ 2D and 3D views: Switch between the model and its UV layout.

▪️ GPU rendering: Preview the finished asset using path tracing and denoising.

▪️ UDIM support: Work with tiled texture sets for more complex assets.

⚡ Performance is a major focus.

TextureCraft uses a tiled, copy-on-write texture engine with multithreaded CPU processing.

Its viewport is powered by wgpu, supporting Vulkan, Metal, DirectX 12, and WebGPU.

The developers report:

▪️ Mesh-map baking approximately 12× faster on GPU than their CPU implementation.

▪️ Path-traced rendering approximately 25× faster in their GPU comparison.

▪️ Responsive painting even with 8K texture sets.

These are project-reported performance figures, not independent comparisons with Substance Painter.

🤖 AI agent integration

TextureCraft also provides a command-line interface and MCP server.

That means AI agents can interact with its tools programmatically rather than manually clicking through the interface.

Possible workflows include preparing materials, baking texture maps, exporting assets, and rendering previews for inspection.

💻 Supported platforms

▪️ Windows

▪️ macOS

▪️ Linux

▪️ FreeBSD

▪️ Browser through WebAssembly

It supports importing formats such as GLB, FBX, OBJ, USD, Alembic, and STL.

Texture exports include PNG, EXR, TIFF, TGA, HDR, and other formats, with options for common game-engine workflows.

Why this matters

Professional 3D texturing remains one of the more specialized parts of game-asset production.

TextureCraft offers another open-source path for artists who want layered PBR painting without being tied to a proprietary tool.

The source code is available under MIT and Apache 2.0 licensing.

And the repository already includes two impressive example assets: a weathered lantern and a vintage rangefinder camera.
